keyVerseText: Is not the whole land before thee? separate thyself, I pray thee, from me: if thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if thou depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left.
rootMeaning: The root of יָמַן (yâman) is a primitive Hebrew root related to being physically right or firm, derived denominatively from יָמִין (yâmîyn), which primarily refers to the right hand, right side, or south. This root conveys not just a direction but a position of strength and dexterity, as the right hand was culturally considered the dominant and more capable side. Thus, beyond the simple English gloss of 'go to the right,' the root implies a deliberate choice toward strength, favor, or authority associated with the right hand.
usageInScripture: The word יָמַן appears four times in Scripture with consistent usage related to directing or using the right hand. Its translations range from 'then I will go to the right,' to 'turn to the right hand,' as well as 'and could use both the right hand,' and simply 'the right hand.' This consistency shows the word’s core meaning involves movement or position toward the right side, often symbolizing choice or favor, and occasionally physical ability or dexterity with the right hand.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding יָמַן enriches our grasp of biblical symbolism where the right hand signifies power, blessing, and divine favor, reflecting God’s sovereign authority and strength. The act of 'going to the right' or choosing the right hand side can represent a righteous or favored path, aligning with God’s will and blessing. For believers, this word reminds us that God’s strength and approval are often symbolized by the right hand, encouraging faithfulness and trust in His guiding power. It highlights the biblical motif that God’s right hand is a place of honor and protection, central to the Christian understanding of divine providence and grace.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 13:9, the phrase 'if you take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if you depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left' uses יָמַן to describe a deliberate choice of direction or side. This word underscores the mutual respect and peaceful separation between Abram and Lot, with each choosing opposite sides to avoid conflict. The right hand here is not just a physical direction but a symbol of choosing a path that honors the other, reflecting God’s desire for harmony and order in relationships.
